passages.title: The moon split and the deniers' turning away
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat open the surah with a single, devastating point: the clearest possible sign was placed in front of the Quraysh — the moon itself split in two over their heads — and they turned away from it. Ayah 1 announces the nearness of the Hour and the miracle that accompanied that announcement; ayat 2–3 record the response of denial; ayat 4–5 remind them that they had already been given news and warning enough, so what was lacking was never the evidence.

## "The Hour has drawn near"

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here informs us of the approach of the Last Hour and the imminent end and demise of this world, and he places the ayah alongside two others: *"The Event ordained by Allah will come to pass, so seek not to hasten it"* (16:1), and *"Draws near for mankind their reckoning, while they turn away in heedlessness"* (21:1). That second ayah is almost a summary of our passage — nearness on one side, turning away on the other.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out how deliberately this opening is joined to what came before. Surah An-Najm had ended on a note of warning to the disbelievers in the words *azifat-il-ʼāzifah* — the Hour of their doom has drawn near; Surah Al-Qamar opens with a similar sentence, followed by one of its proofs: the appearance of the miracle of the moon being split asunder.

**How near is near?** Ibn Kathir gathers several hadiths of this meaning. Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr Al-Bazzar recorded that Anas said that one day, when the sun was about to set, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to his Companions, *"By He in Whose Hand is my soul! Not much of this world is left compared to what has already passed of it, except as much as what is left in this day of yours compared to what has already passed of it."* Anas added, "We could only see a small part of the setting sun at the time."

Ibn Kathir then gives a hadith that supports and explains it, recorded by Imam Ahmad from ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar, who said they were sitting with the Prophet ﷺ after ʿAsr, the sun rising above Quʿayqaʿan, when he ﷺ said, *"What remains of your time, compared to what has passed, is as long as what remains of this day compared to what has passed of it."*

Imam Ahmad also recorded from Sahl bin Saʿd that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, *"I was sent like this with the Last Hour"* — and he pointed with his middle and index finger. Ibn Kathir notes that the Two Sahihs also recorded this hadith. In another narration Imam Ahmad recorded from Wahb As-Suwaʿi that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"I was sent just before the Last Hour, like the distance between this and this; the latter almost overtook the former"* — and Al-Aʿmash joined his index and middle fingers while narrating it. And Imam Ahmad alone collected the report from Anas bin Malik, asked by Al-Walid bin ʿAbdul-Malik what he had heard about the Last Hour, that he ﷺ said, *"You and the Last Hour are as close as these two (fingers)."* Ibn Kathir adds a further support: among the names of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ listed in the Sahih is *Al-Hashir*, literally the Gatherer — he is the first to be gathered, and all people will be gathered thereafter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same connection from its own angle: one of the many signs of the Day of Doom is the advent of the last of the Prophets ﷺ himself, as reported in the hadith *"I was sent like this with the last Hour"* — and he pointed with his middle and index fingers.

## The night the moon was split

The second half of ayah 1 states a fact about something that had already happened in Makkah. Ibn Kathir is unambiguous: it occurred during the time of Allah's Messenger ﷺ, according to the authentic *mutawātir* hadiths, and it was among the clear miracles that Allah gave him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the Companions through whom it comes: ʿAbdullah Ibn Masʿud, ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿUmar, Jubair Ibn Mutʿim, ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas Ibn Malik and others, and notes that ʿAbdullah Ibn Masʿud reports he himself was present and witnessed it. It adds that Imams Tahawi and Ibn Kathir have both stated that the reports of the moon-splitting are *mutawatir* — reported successively and uninterruptedly by such a large number of authorities that their concurrence on falsehood is inconceivable — so that this prophetic miracle has been proved by incontrovertible evidence.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pulls the narrations into a single scene. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting at Mina in Makkah. The pagans demanded that he produce a proof substantiating his claim. It was a moonlit night. Allah split the moon into two parts — a part over one mountain on the eastern side, another part over another mountain on the western side, so that a mountain stood between the two parts. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to all who were present: *"Be witnesses."* When all the people had seen the miracle clearly, the two pieces rejoined. It was not possible, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, for any person with eyes to deny this clear miracle. It also notes that some reports indicate the miracle occurred twice, but that more authentic reports confirm it occurred once only, citing *Bayan-ul-Quran*.

Al-Bukhari recorded from Anas bin Malik that the people of Makkah asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to produce a miracle, and he showed them the splitting of the moon into two parts, until they saw the mount of Hira' between them — Ibn Kathir notes this hadith is recorded in the Two Sahihs with various chains of narration. Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas bin Malik that the people of Makkah asked the Prophet ﷺ for a miracle and the moon was split into two parts in Makkah, and Allah said, *"The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has been cleft asunder"*; Muslim also collected this hadith. Al-Bukhari recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas simply, "The moon was split during the time of the Prophet ﷺ" — a hadith Al-Bukhari and Muslim collected — and Ibn Jarir records Ibn ʿAbbas commenting on ayat 1–2: "This occurred before the Hijrah; the moon was split and they saw it in two parts."

From Ibn Masʿud, Imam Ahmad recorded: "The moon was split in two parts during the time of Allah's Messenger, and they saw its two parts," and Allah's Messenger ﷺ said, *"Be witnesses"* — a hadith Al-Bukhari and Muslim collected. Imam Ahmad also records him saying, "The moon was split during the time of Allah's Messenger ﷺ and I saw the mount between its two parts." In the version Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites from Ibn Jarir he says: "We were with Allah's Messenger ﷺ at Mina. Suddenly the moon split in two pieces, and one piece went away behind the mountain. Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: 'Be witnesses; be witnesses.'" And Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr Al-Bayhaqi recorded that ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar said of this ayah: "This occurred during the time of Allah's Messenger ﷺ; the moon was split in two parts. A part of it was before the mount and a part on the other side," and the Prophet ﷺ said, *"O Allah! Be witness."* Ibn Kathir notes that this is the narration Muslim and At-Tirmidhi collected, and that At-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan Sahih."

## "Magic that will pass"

The reaction comes in ayah 2. Ibn Kathir glosses *"And if they see an Ayah"* as: if they see proof, evidence and a sign. *"They turn away"*, he says, means they do not believe in it; rather, they turn away from it, abandoning it behind their backs.

Their verdict was *siḥrun mustamirr*. Ibn Kathir reports what they were saying: "the sign that we saw was magic, which was cast on us." As for *mustamir*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that in the popular sense of the word as used in Persian and Urdu it means something lasting or enduring, but in Arabic it is sometimes used in the sense of passing away or coming to an end, being derived from *marra* and *istamarra*. Ibn Kathir reports that *mustamir* means "will soon go away" according to Mujahid, Qatadah and several others: the Quraysh said that the cleaving of the moon was false and would soon diminish and fade away. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows the same reading through Mujahid and Qatadah, and adds that another meaning of the word is strong and firm, which is how Abul-ʿAliyah and Dahhak interpreted it — meaning that this is a very potent sorcery. Both readings arrive at the same refusal: whether they called it flimsy or called it formidable, they would not call it a sign from Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records how they tried to manage the problem. The pagans said: "Muhammad has ensorcelled us, but he cannot bewitch the whole world; so let us wait for people to come from the neighbouring parts of the country and hear what they have to say" — reported from Baihaqi and Abu Dawud Tayalisi. In the fuller wording of Ibn Masʿud's narration recorded by Baihaqi and Abu Dawud Tayalisi, the disbelieving Quraysh said: "This is sorcery… therefore, wait for the neighbouring travellers to arrive. If they too have seen the two pieces of the moon, then he has spoken the truth. But if they have not seen the parts of the moon, then this is indeed a magical illusion which he has performed on you." When the travellers arrived and were asked, they all confirmed that they did see the two parts of the moon.

Imam Ahmad recorded something similar from Jubayr bin Mutʿim: the moon was split into two pieces during the time of Allah's Prophet ﷺ, a part of the moon over one mountain and another part over another mountain, and they said, "Muhammad ﷺ has taken us by his magic," then added, "If he was able to take us by magic, he will not be able to do so with all people." Ibn Kathir notes that only Imam Ahmad recorded this hadith with this chain of narration, and that Al-Bayhaqi used another chain of narration in a similar hadith he collected in *Ad-Dalāʼil*.

Ayah 3 states the outcome plainly: *"They denied and followed their own lusts."* Ibn Kathir explains that they rejected the truth when it came to them, following the ignorance and foolishness that their lusts and desires called them to.

## "And every matter will be settled"

The second half of ayah 3, *wa kullu amrin mustaqirr*, lands like a gavel. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the literal meaning of *istiqrār* is to settle: the ayah means that everything must ultimately reach its end and the matter must become clear — if a veil is fabricated and cast over the truth or reality, eventually, in its designated time, the false veil will be removed and truth and falsehood will be clearly distinguished.

Ibn Kathir reports the early explanations side by side. According to Qatadah it means good deeds will take their doers to all that is good and righteous, and similarly evil deeds will take their doers to all that is evil. Ibn Jurayj said it "will settle according to its people." Mujahid commented on it by saying: "On the Day of Resurrection."

## Warning that was never in short supply

Ayah 4 answers a defence the deniers might have raised: were we ever really told? *"And indeed there has come to them news…"* — Ibn Kathir explains this as the news, in this Qur'an, of the earlier nations that disbelieved in their Messengers and the torment, punishment and affliction that befell them. The word *muzdajar* he glosses as: wherein there are warnings and lessons to stop them from idolatry and persisting in denial.

Ayah 5 then names what all of this is: *ḥikmatun bālighah*, perfect wisdom. Ibn Kathir reads it as perfect wisdom in that Allah guides whomever He wills and misguides whomever He wills. Then the closing clause: *"but warners benefit them not."* Ibn Kathir explains that the preaching of warnings does not benefit those upon whom Allah has written misery and sealed their hearts — and he asks: who can guide such people after Allah? He supports this with two ayat of the same register: *"Say: 'With Allah is the perfect proof and argument; had He so willed, He would indeed have guided you all'"* (6:149), and *"But neither Ayat nor warners benefit those who believe not"* (10:101).

## The objections raised later

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes up two kinds of criticism of the moon-splitting: one based on the assumptions of Greek philosophers, the other on layman's thinking.

The deviant Greek philosophers assume that it is not possible for the heaven and other celestial bodies to split or crack and rejoin. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that this is merely an idea unsubstantiated by any solid or concrete proof, and that the Islamic theologians (*mutakallimīn*) have broken down their arguments and shown them to be baseless. It adds a point worth remembering: illiterate people regard every unusual thing as impossible, whereas the very meaning of a *muʿjizah*, a prophetic miracle, is that it is an unusual event, out of the general habit of things, which cannot be performed by common people.

The second objection is the layman's: if such a wonderful event had taken place, its knowledge would be commonplace and would be mentioned in the books of history. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān replies that such thinking is too simplistic. The event occurred in Makkah at night: in many parts of the world it must have been daytime, where the question of witnessing it does not even arise, and in many other countries it must have been the middle or last part of the night when people normally sleep. Furthermore, people who are awake do not stare at the moon all the time, and the splitting of the moon would not have made any difference to the moonlight spread on the earth such that it would attract attention. The event took place suddenly and lasted for a short while. Compare a lunar eclipse: nowadays a forecast is made about its occurrence well in advance, yet there are hundreds of thousands of people absolutely unaware of it — which is no proof that the eclipse did not take place. So if the event is not recorded in world history books, its occurrence cannot on that basis be denied.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the event is recorded in the well-known history book of India called *Tarikh-e-Farishtah*, which mentions that the Maharajah, a native ruler of Malabar, had witnessed this phenomenon that night with his own eyes and had it entered in his diary, and that this incident was the cause of his embracing Islam. It closes with: "Allah, the Pure and the Exalted, knows best!"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also draws out why this particular miracle suits a surah about the Hour: just as Allah's power split the moon into two, so will planets and stars be destroyed by Him, broken into very small pieces — which is not impossible, as has been proved by the miracle of splitting the moon.

Ibn Kathir opens the surah with a related note: the hadith of Abu Waqid preceded, in which it is mentioned that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would recite Surah Qaf and *Iqtarabat As-Sāʿah*, this surah, during the ʿId prayers of Al-Adha and Al-Fitr. He used to recite these two surahs during major gatherings and occasions because they contain Allah's promises and warnings, and information about the origin of creation, the Resurrection, Tawhid, the affirmation of prophethood, and other such great objectives.

## What the passage asks of us

**Evidence alone does not settle a heart.** The Quraysh saw the moon in two parts with a mountain between them, ran their own verification with the arriving travellers, and the ayah's verdict on them is *"They denied and followed their own lusts."* Before we place ourselves among the believers of that night, the honest question is where our own conclusions are being quietly set by what we want to be true.

**Turning away is a posture, not an argument.** Ibn Kathir's description of *"they turn away"*: they do not believe in it; rather they turn away from it, abandoning it behind their backs. Registering something and then leaving it behind one's back is a move available to anyone, in any century.

**Keep the Hour in view.** *"I was sent like this with the Last Hour,"* said the Prophet ﷺ, pointing with his middle and index finger. And when the sun was nearly down he ﷺ told his Companions that what is left of this world compared with what has passed is only like what is left of this day compared with what has passed of it. That is proportion, not panic — and it is where Ibn Kathir chooses to begin this surah.

**The testimony travelled.** "Be witnesses," he ﷺ said, and "O Allah! Be witness." What those present saw came down through ʿAbdullah Ibn Masʿud, ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿUmar, Jubair Ibn Mutʿim, ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas Ibn Malik and others — reported, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says citing Imams Tahawi and Ibn Kathir, by so large a number of authorities that their concurrence on falsehood is inconceivable. The night at Mina reaches us as testimony, still intact.

passages.title: The Day the caller summons them from the graves
passages.tafsir:
Three ayat, one unbroken picture. A sign has been shown and rejected; the Prophet ﷺ is told to turn away from the deniers and to wait for the Day when a caller summons them out of their graves. What holds ayat 6–8 together is a single scene: one command to turn away, then one long look at what follows — the call, the emerging, the rushing, and finally the words that break out of the disbelievers' own mouths.

## "So turn away from them" — ayah 6

Ibn Kathir sets the command in its immediate context. Allah the Exalted says, in his paraphrase, "O Muhammad, turn away from these people who, when they witness a miracle, they deny it and say that this is continuous magic." That is the situation: a sign has been given, and instead of yielding to it the deniers have filed it under sorcery — not even a one-off trick, but magic that keeps on going. When a heart has decided in advance what it will not accept, the evidence does not reach it; the evidence simply gets renamed.

And then Ibn Kathir gives the shape of the command in a single line: "Turn away from them and wait until…" — and what follows the *until* is not another argument to be made. It is a Day.

## The caller and the "terrible thing"

*Yawma yadʿu al-dāʿ* — "the Day the caller calls." The commentary does not pause to identify the caller; all of its attention goes to what the call is *to*.

The ayah says *ilā shayʾin nukur* — to "a thing terrible." Ibn Kathir explains it as "the Recompense and the afflictions, horrors and tremendous hardships that it brings forth." Notice that the destination is left almost anonymous — a *thing*. Nothing in ordinary experience furnishes a name for it, so the Qur'an gives it none. It is horror without a category.

There is a quiet irony running under the ayah. In this life these people saw a sign and called it magic. On that Day a call goes out to a reality that admits no such renaming — and, as we are about to see, no one is able even to slow his step in answering it.

## Out of the graves like scattered locusts — ayah 7

Ayah 7 opens with the eyes: *khushshaʿan abṣāruhum* — "with humbled eyes," "eyes downcast." Ibn Kathir's gloss is one short phrase and it is devastating: "their eyes will be covered with disgrace." The eye is where a person's confidence shows. These are the same people who witnessed a miracle and called it magic; now the look is gone out of them before a word of the reckoning has been spoken. This is not yet the punishment — Ibn Kathir places the scene on the way to the area of Reckoning — and already they cannot lift their gaze.

Then: *yakhrujūna min al-ajdāth* — "they come forth from the graves." The verb is plain, almost physical. The graves that seemed to be the end of the story turn out to be a doorway.

And then the image: *kaʾannahum jarādun muntashir* — "as if they were locusts spread abroad." Ibn Kathir draws out what the comparison is doing: "They will gather towards the area of Reckoning in such haste and crowds, in response to the caller, as if they were crowds of locusts spreading all about."

Two things come through the image at once. The first is **numbers** — Ibn Kathir's word is *crowds*, twice over; a locust swarm is uncountable, all horizon, no gaps. The second is **movement in one direction**: a swarm does not deliberate, and no locust in it is going anywhere of its own choosing. Nothing of the personal survives into that scene except what will be judged.

It is worth pausing on how economical this is. The passage does not describe the Fire. It describes a crowd walking, and lets that do the work.

## Rushing, heads up — ayah 8

*Muhṭiʿīna ilā al-dāʿ* — "hastening towards the caller." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word: *muhṭiʿ* "literally denotes walking quickly with one's head raised above." So this is not a shuffle. It is a fast, fixed, neck-craned movement — the whole body pulled toward the source of the voice.

Ibn Kathir adds the crucial point about what kind of haste it is. *Muhṭiʿīn*, he says, means "hurriedly," and they move toward the caller "without being able to hesitate or slow down." This is speed without willingness. They are not eager; they are unable to do anything else. Everything that once let a person delay — postponement, distraction, the ability to say *not yet, next year, when I am older* — has been withdrawn. In this life the whole machinery of denial runs on delay. On that Day the delay is simply not available.

**A question the sources answer directly.** In ayah 7 their eyes are cast down; in ayah 8 they walk with heads raised. Is that not a contradiction? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the question up and settles it: the two verses are "in no conflict … because there will be many different occasions in *maḥshar*" — the vast gathering-place of the Reckoning — and "on some of these occasions, the eyes of all the people will be cast down." The Day is not a single instant with a single posture. It is long, and it has stages; the Qur'an shows us more than one of them in consecutive lines. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this verse together with the two preceding ones gives "a graphic picture of the Day of Gathering or Reckoning," in which "the people will hasten hurriedly in the direction of the voice of the Caller towards the *maḥshar*."

Held together, the two postures are one portrait: the head is up because the body is being carried forward and cannot stop; the eyes are down because there is nothing they wish to see.

## "This is a hard Day"

The passage ends by handing the words to the deniers themselves: *yaqūlu al-kāfirūna hādhā yawmun ʿasir* — "The disbelievers will say: 'This is a hard Day.'" Ibn Kathir renders their meaning: "this is a hard, terrible, horrifying and distressful Day."

No refutation is offered them, no argument is won over them. They arrive at the verdict on their own, out loud, in the middle of the crowd. What they had called continuous magic has become the ground under their feet, and the first thing they say about it is that it is *hard*.

Ibn Kathir brings a second passage of the Qur'an alongside it: *"Truly, that Day will be a Hard Day — far from easy for the disbelievers"* (74:9–10). The pairing is precise, and the added phrase matters: hard, and "far from easy" **for the disbelievers** specifically. It is the same Day for everyone; what differs is who you arrive as.

## Living it

**Learn when to stop arguing.** The instruction in ayah 6 is to turn away and to wait. For anyone who has worn themselves out trying to convince someone who has already decided what they will not accept, there is relief in that: the truth has been delivered, and what happens next is not on your shoulders to force. The answer to the mockery, in this passage, is not another round of debate. It is a Day.

**Do not confuse a delay with a verdict.** Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is "turn away from them and wait until…" — the sentence has an *until* in it. Nothing happening yet is a statement about timing, not about the outcome.

**Watch what happens to the eyes.** Whatever a person's confidence rests on in this world, ayah 7 shows the look draining out of the face before the reckoning has even begun — "their eyes will be covered with disgrace." That is worth checking your own confidence against now, while there is still time to relocate it.

**Answer the caller now, while answering is still a choice.** The tragedy of ayah 8 is not the speed; it is that the speed is compelled — "without being able to hesitate or slow down." Every summons of the truth answered while refusal was still possible is the same movement made freely, and it is the free version that counts.

passages.title: Noah's people, the flood, and the Ark
passages.tafsir:
These nine ayat tell the first of the surah's warning-stories: a people who called their prophet a madman, a prophet who finally cried out to his Lord, and a flood that answered. What holds the passage together is a single movement from denial to destruction to deliverance — and then, in ayat 15–17, a turn away from the story toward the listener: *is there anyone who will take heed?*

## "Before them" — why this story, and why now

The passage opens with a comparison built into its first word. Ibn Kathir glosses **كَذَّبَتْ** — "they denied" — with the sense: *'before your people, O Muhammad.'* The denial being met now has a precedent; the people of Nuh had already walked this road. So this is not merely history. It is addressed to the audience of the Qur'an, which is why the passage ends not with the flood but with a question put to whoever is listening.

## "A madman!" — and the word wazdujir

Ibn Kathir explains **فَكَذَّبُوا عَبْدَنَا** — "they rejected Our servant" — as meaning that they denied him categorically and accused him of madness. The harder word is **وَازْدُجِرَ** (*wazdujir*). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that it literally means *he was rebuked*, and refers to the attitude of Nuh's people, who rebuked and threatened him to stop him from preaching. Ibn Kathir records two readings:

- **Mujahid** said of *wazdujir*: "He was driven out accused on account of madness" — social expulsion, the man pushed to the margins as a lunatic.
- It was also said that it means he was rebuked, deterred, threatened and warned by his people, as in their words recorded elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"If you do not stop, O Nuh, you will be among those who will be stoned"* (26:116). Ibn Kathir attributes this to Ibn Zayd and comments that "it is sound."

The two are not really rivals. Between them they sketch the full arc of persecution: first the character assassination, then the threat of violence. And note the form of the word as both tafsirs render it — *he was rebuked*, passive. Nuh is the one being acted upon.

## Nine hundred and fifty years of restraint

This is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the passage up most. It reports that ʿAbd ibn Humayd relates from Mujahid that when some of his people found Nuh somewhere, they would choke him until he lost consciousness. When he recovered, he would pray to Allah:

> "O Allah! Forgive my people, for they do not know the truth."

In this way he endured the persecution of his people patiently for nine hundred and fifty years, praying for their forgiveness and for their understanding of the truth. Eventually, when the situation became intolerable and he could no longer resist his people, he invoked Allah to help him against them.

Hold that next to ayah 10 and the ayah changes shape. **فَدَعَا رَبَّهُ أَنِّي مَغْلُوبٌ فَانتَصِرْ** — "So he called upon his Lord: I have been overcome, so help!" This is not a man with a short fuse. It is the last word of someone who had absorbed nine and a half centuries of abuse, and who between beatings was asking Allah to *forgive* the people beating him.

And look at what he actually asks for. Ibn Kathir renders the sense: *'I am weak and cannot overcome or resist my people, so help Your religion!'* He confesses his own helplessness — **مَغْلُوبٌ**, *overcome* — and the help he asks for is help for Allah's religion. The servant admits he has nothing left; the Lord takes it from there.

## The flood: heaven and earth acting on one order

The answer comes in ayat 11–12, and the language is deliberately overwhelming.

**فَفَتَحْنَا أَبْوَابَ السَّمَاءِ بِمَاءٍ مُّنْهَمِرٍ** — "So We opened the gates of the sky with water *munhamir*." As-Suddi said *munhamir* means **abundant**. Ibn Jurayj reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that this was torrential rain: the only water that fell from the sky before that day and ever since was from clouds, but the sky's gates were opened upon them that day, so the water that came down was not from clouds.

Then the ground joins in: **وَفَجَّرْنَا الْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا** — "and We caused the earth to burst forth with springs." Ibn Kathir explains this means from every part of the earth; even ovens in which fire was burning gushed with water and springs. That detail is worth pausing on — the one place on earth where water could not be, the lit oven, became a spring. There was no refuge left in the physics of the world.

**فَالْتَقَى الْمَاءُ عَلَىٰ أَمْرٍ قَدْ قُدِرَ** — "so the waters met for a matter already decreed." Ibn Kathir: the water of the heaven and the water of the earth. Ibn ʿAbbas's report ends on the same note: both waters met "according to a matter ordained." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the picture out — the rain pouring down from the skies in torrents together with the water bubbling up from under the ground caused the Deluge that engulfed the entire land, so the Divine decree was fulfilled: the people of Nuh were destroyed to the last man, and even the peaks of the mountains could not give them any shelter.

The weight sits in that phrase **أَمْرٍ قَدْ قُدِرَ**. Two vast forces converge from opposite directions at exactly the right moment — not chaos, but an appointment kept. Nuh waited 950 years; the water arrived on schedule.

## The Ark: planks and nails

Against all that water, ayah 13 describes the vessel with almost startling modesty: **ذَاتِ أَلْوَاحٍ وَدُسُرٍ** — "one of planks and *dusur*."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the vocabulary: **alwāḥ** is the plural of *lawḥ*, a board or a plank; **dusur** is the plural of *disār*, meaning a nail — and it can also mean a cord of palm-tree fibres with which the planks of a ship are bound together. Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Qurazi, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd all said *dusur* means nails, and that Ibn Jarir preferred this view.

The Qur'an does not describe a mighty ship. It lists the raw materials: wood and fasteners. What saved Nuh was not the engineering. That is made explicit in ayah 14: **تَجْرِي بِأَعْيُنِنَا** — "sailing under Our Eyes." Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: *by Our command and under Our protection and observation.* The Ark was not drifting. It moved by His command, watched and guarded — and a raft of planks and nails is enough when it sails like that.

Then the reason: **جَزَاءً لِّمَن كَانَ كُفِرَ** — "a recompense for the one who had been rejected." Ibn Kathir reads this in both directions at once: it was recompense *for them* because of their disbelief in Allah, and reward *for Nuh*, peace be upon him. One event, two verdicts. The same water that was punishment for the deniers was the vehicle of rescue for the servant they had denied.

## "We left it as a sign"

Ayah 15: **وَلَقَد تَّرَكْنَاهَا آيَةً** — "And We certainly left this as a sign." The scholars differ over what "it" refers to, and both views deserve to be heard:

- **Qatadah** said that Allah left the ship of Nuh intact until the first generation of this Ummah were able to see it — the actual vessel preserved as a standing witness.
- **Ibn Kathir** says that it appears the meaning here is that Allah kept *ships* as a sign. He supports this with other ayat — "And a sign for them is that We bore their offspring in the laden ship. And We have created for them of the like thereunto, on which they ride" (36:41–42), and "Verily, when the water rose beyond its limits, We carried you in the boat, that We might make it an admonition for you, and that it might be retained by the retaining ears" (69:11–12).

On this second reading, the sign is not in a museum. The ayat Ibn Kathir cites point at the vessels people ride now: what floats today is of the same kind as what carried them then, and is meant to be taken as an admonition.

## The question that will not let you go: fahal min muddakir

Ayah 15 closes with **فَهَلْ مِن مُّدَّكِرٍ** — "so is there any who will remember?" Ibn Kathir explains: is there any who will receive admonition and reminder?

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad reported from ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud that the Prophet ﷺ recited to him **فَهَلْ مِن مُّدَّكِرٍ**. Al-Bukhari collected a similar hadith from ʿAbdullah, that he said: "I recited to the Prophet ﷺ *fahal min mudhdhakir*, and the Prophet ﷺ said: *fahal min muddakir*." A small, precise correction of a single letter — the Companion read it back to the Prophet ﷺ and was corrected on a consonant.

Ayah 16 then turns the story into a direct address: **فَكَيْفَ كَانَ عَذَابِي وَنُذُرِ** — "So how were My punishment and My warnings!" Ibn Kathir unpacks the double sense: how terrible was the torment inflicted on those who disbelieved in Allah and denied His Messengers and did not heed His warnings — and how was His help extended to His Messengers, and the retribution exerted on their behalf? It is at once a threat to the deniers and a promise to anyone standing where Nuh stood.

## Ayah 17: the Qur'an made easy — and what "easy" does not mean

The passage ends where the surah keeps returning: **وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ فَهَلْ مِن مُّدَّكِرٍ** — "And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance; so is there any who will remember?"

Ibn Kathir explains: We have made the Qur'an easy to recite and to comprehend for those who seek these traits, to remind mankind. He connects it to "(This is) a Book which We have sent down to you, full of blessings, that they may ponder over its ayat, and that men of understanding may remember" (38:29), and "So We have made this easy in your own tongue, only that you may give glad tidings to those who have taqwa and warn with it the most quarrelsome people" (19:97). And on "is there any who will remember," Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi commented simply: **"Is there anyone who will avoid evil?"** — remembrance that does not change behaviour is not what the ayah is asking for.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the word **لِلذِّكْرِ**. *Dhikr* here carries several shades — to remember, to memorise, to hold by heart; and to take heed of admonition and warnings — and both meanings are equally applicable here.

On the first: Allah has made this Book easy to memorise. The followers of the previous scriptures were not privileged to memorise their entire book word by word — whether Torah, Injil or Zabur. It is one of the privileges conferred on Muslims that He has made it easy even for tender-aged children to commit the entire Qur'an to memory, word for word, without missing out a single letter; and it has been preserved in the hearts of hundreds of thousands of huffaz for the past fourteen hundred years, in every age, among people of every level, in every region of the world.

On the second: the Qur'an has been made so simple that just as an intellectual and knowledgeable person benefits from its contents, so does a layman with no expertise in the relevant sciences — he too benefits from its admonition and warnings, at his own level.

**An important limit.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the verb *yassarnā* ("We have made easy") is qualified by *lidh-dhikr* ("for remembrance"). This implies that the Qur'an has been made easy to the extent of memorising it and paying heed to its advice and warnings — a benefit open to scholar and unlearned person, young and old. It does not follow that the derivation of laws and injunctions from the Qur'an is easy for everybody. *Ijtihad* and *istinbat* — independent legal reasoning and the deduction of rulings — form a science with its own complex rules; scholars well-grounded in knowledge have spent years of their lives to attain the position where they could exercise them. It is not a field where every ordinary person can play his role. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the error plainly: some deviant people, on the strength of this statement, wish to pose as mujtahids and derive rulings by their own reasoning, without acquiring complete and profound knowledge of the Qur'an and without fully grasping its methodological principles. That, it says, is clear deviation.

## Living it

The passage asks three things of a reader, and each of them comes straight out of the text:

**Pray for the people who are hardest on you, before you pray against them.** Nuh's recorded response to being choked unconscious was to ask Allah to forgive his people, because they did not know the truth. The prayer of ayah 10 came only after that patience had been exhausted — and even then the help he sought was help for Allah's religion.

**Say "I am overcome" honestly.** *Innī maghlūb* is not a failure of faith; it is a servant naming his weakness before the only One who can do something about it. Ibn Kathir's reading — *I am weak and cannot overcome or resist my people, so help Your religion* — turns helplessness into worship.

**Answer the question.** Twice in these ayat Allah asks, "Is there any who will remember?" Al-Qurazi's answer is the practical one: the person who remembers is the person who avoids evil. And ayah 17 says the way in is open — the Book has been made easy to carry in the heart and easy to be warned by, whoever you are.

passages.title: 'Ād destroyed by the furious wind
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat tell, in the space of a few breaths, the entire story of a civilisation: 'Ād denied the Messenger sent to them, a wind was sent against them, and a people counted among the strongest of their day were plucked out of the earth like uprooted stems of date palms. What holds the passage together is a rhythm rather than a narrative — a denial (ayah 18), a punishment described in two swift strokes (ayat 19–20), and then two refrains that close the account: **"Then how were My punishment and warnings!"** (ayah 21) and **"And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy to remember. So is there any who will remember?"** (ayah 22).

## Where this sits in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the design of Sūrah al-Qamar as a whole, and it makes this passage far easier to read. The sūrah opens on the note that the Day of Judgement is fast approaching — meant to bring to their senses those who were full of lust and greed for this world and unaware of the Hereafter. First the punishment of the Hereafter is mentioned. Then the evil consequences of their misdeeds in the present life are cited, with reference made to world-famous nations, their opposition to their respective prophets, and what that opposition cost them. Their stories are recounted in detail on several occasions in the Qur'an; here, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, they have been condensed.

That is why the account of 'Ād is so compressed. It is not the whole story of Hūd (peace be upon him) and his people; it is one exhibit in a sequence of exhibits. Ibn Kathir's very first comment on ayah 18 makes the connection explicit: Allah states that 'Ād, the People of Hūd, denied their Messenger, **just as the people of Nūḥ did**. The denial is the thread that runs from one nation to the next.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the point that makes the sequence bite. All of the nations named in this sūrah were the strongest and most resourceful. It was not possible for any of the subdued nations to overcome any of these superpowers. And this set of verses shows precisely those superpowers being destroyed by divine punishment — nations very powerful in might, wealth and number, killed, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, like flies and mosquitoes. The point is not that weak or marginal peoples were swept away. It is that the mightiest were.

## Ayah 18: "'Ād rejected"

**"'Ād ˹also˺ rejected ˹the truth˺. Then how ˹dreadful˺ were My punishment and warnings!"**

The verb that opens the passage is *kadhdhabat* — rendered "rejected," and by Ibn Kathir simply "denied." Ibn Kathir specifies the object: they denied their Messenger. Notice how little else the ayah says. No list of their sins, no catalogue of their crimes. The one fact that decides their fate is that a messenger came and they denied him.

Then, before a single detail of the punishment is given, the refrain arrives: *fa-kayfa kāna ʿadhābī wa-nudhur* — "Then how were My punishment and warnings!" It stands here at the end of ayah 18 and appears again, word for word, as the whole of ayah 21, framing the punishment on both sides. Placed first, it is a question thrown at the listener before he has even been told what happened: *now watch what that denial produced.*

The refrain also pairs two things that we tend to separate. *ʿAdhābī* — "My punishment" — is joined to *nudhur*, "My warnings." A messenger had stood among them, and it was his denial that Ibn Kathir names as the cause. The destruction in ayah 19 is the second half of a sentence whose first half was a messenger sent.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that after describing the punishment of each nation, the Qur'an repeats this exact statement as a refrain — it is the line that turns several separate histories into one argument.

## Ayah 19: the wind that was sent

**"Indeed, We sent against them a furious wind, on a day of unrelenting misfortune."**

Three words carry this ayah, and each one deepens the horror.

**رِيحٗا صَرۡصَرٗا — *rīḥan ṣarṣaran*.** Ibn Kathir glosses *ṣarṣar* as a **bitterly cold and furious wind**. Both halves of that gloss matter: it is not merely a storm of force, but a cold one. And note what the ayah says was done with it — "We sent against them"; in Ibn Kathir's words, "So, Allah sent on them." It was not weather that merely happened to them. It was sent.

**فِي يَوۡمِ نَحۡسٖ — *fī yawmi naḥsin*, "on a day of calamity."** Ibn Kathir reports this understanding — that the day was one of calamity **against them** — from three early authorities of tafsir: **aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, and as-Suddī**. That small qualification, "against them," is worth pausing on. What the words fix upon is not a day unlucky in itself, as though certain squares on a calendar carried misfortune, but a day of calamity *for those people* — because of what fell upon them on it.

**مُّسۡتَمِرّٖ — *mustamirr*, "continuous."** This is the word that stretches the punishment past the horizon. Ibn Kathir explains that it was continuous upon them because the calamity, torment and destruction that they suffered in this life on that day **continued with that of the Hereafter**. The wind stopped; the punishment did not. What the reader is being shown in ayah 19 is not the end of 'Ād's story but the opening of it — a single day in this world that runs on into the next.

That reading also ties this passage back to the structure Maʿārif ul Qurʼān described: the sūrah first mentions the punishment of the Hereafter, then turns to the evil consequences in this present life. In *mustamirr*, the two meet in one word.

## Ayah 20: like uprooted stems of date palms

**"that snatched people up, leaving them like trunks of uprooted palm trees."**

Ibn Kathir's rendering is *"Plucking out men as if they were uprooted stems of date palms."* Human beings, who stand on the earth, are described as being pulled out of it.

Ibn Kathir describes what this looked like: the wind would pluck one of them and raise him high, until he could no longer be seen, and then violently send him down on his head to the ground. His head would be smashed, and only his body would be left — headless.

That detail explains the image the ayah chooses. **كَأَنَّهُمۡ أَعۡجَازُ نَخۡلٖ مُّنقَعِرٖ** — "as if they were uprooted stems of date palms." A stem torn out of the ground and lying on its side is exactly the shape of what the wind left behind: a body with no head, no longer standing, no longer rooted, lying where it fell.

Hold this next to the observation from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān that these nations were the strongest and most resourceful, whom no subdued nation could have overcome. Their strength was real. Against this wind, it counted for nothing.

## Ayah 21: the question repeated

**"Then how ˹dreadful˺ were My punishment and warnings!"**

The same words as the end of ayah 18, now on the other side of the description. Before, it was a question the listener could not yet answer. Now he has seen the answer — and the form is not really a request for information at all. It is a question posed for effect: *look at what it was.*

Repeating it on both sides of the story makes the punishment the frame of the passage, not merely its content. And by joining "My warnings" to "My punishment" a second time, the ayah keeps the two together in the listener's mind. A messenger was sent before a wind was.

## Ayah 22: the door left open

**"And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy to remember. So is there any who will remember?"**

After the wind and the headless bodies, this is where the passage lands — and it is mercy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this verse is repeated to advise the Muslims and the disbelievers in general, and that it indicates that **the only way to avoid the terrible chastisement is to take to the advice of the Qur'an**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it: *"and indeed We have made the Qur'an easy for seeking advice. So, is there one to seek advice?"*

Notice the scope of the ease being claimed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is precise: Allah has made the Qur'an easy **to the extent of paying heed to the admonition and warnings**. That is a claim about the accessibility of its warning, not a promise that every subtlety of the Book is effortless. You may need a lifetime and a teacher to master its law and its language. But you do not need any of that to grasp *this*: nations far mightier than you denied their messengers and were destroyed; take warning. That much is within reach of anyone who will listen. Ibn Kathir's rendering carries a double sense — the Qur'an has been made easy both **to understand and to remember**.

Which is why Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes as sharply as it does: only the most ill-fated person will not take advantage of the warnings. The excuse of difficulty has been removed. What remains is willingness.

And the phrasing of the question is itself an invitation. *Fa-hal min muddakir* — "so is there any who will remember?" It is left hanging in the air of the sūrah, waiting for someone to step forward and answer it.

## What this asks of us

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the application that the sūrah itself makes next. The forthcoming verses address the people of the time of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with a plain comparison: they are not more powerful in wealth, number and might than the people of Lūṭ (peace be upon him), the tribes of 'Ād and Thamūd, or the people of Firʿawn. **Then how are they sitting in a careless manner?**

That question was not exhausted by the generation it was first addressed to. Every reader who treats stability, prosperity or power as a kind of insurance is standing where 'Ād stood. So three things follow from this passage:

- **Take the warning as personally addressed.** The histories are condensed here — told at length elsewhere in the Qur'an — so that they land as argument, not as antiquarian interest.
- **Do not measure your safety by your strength.** The whole force of the passage is that the strongest were destroyed. Security lies in heeding the One who warns, not in resources.
- **Answer the question in ayah 22.** The Qur'an has been made easy for exactly this purpose — for taking heed of the admonition and the warnings. The reader who reaches the end of this passage and simply moves on has heard the question and declined to be the one who remembers.

passages.title: Thamūd, the she-camel, and the single blast
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** These ten ayat tell the story of Thamūd: a people who refused their prophet because he was an ordinary man from among them, who were then given a sign they had themselves asked for, and who killed it. The arc runs from a sneer in ayah 24 to total silence in ayah 31, sealed by the surah's two refrains — "Then, how was My torment and My warnings?" (ayah 30) and "And indeed, We have made the Qur'an easy to understand and remember; then is there any that will remember?" (ayah 32).

## Why Thamūd is being told here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the frame. Sūrah al-Qamar opens on the note that the Day of Judgement is fast approaching, so that people absorbed in this world and unaware of the Hereafter might come to their senses. First the punishment of the Hereafter is mentioned; then the evil consequences of their misdeeds in this present life are cited, through the conditions of world-famous nations — ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lūṭ, the people of Firʿawn — their opposition to their prophets and what came of it. Their stories are recounted in detail elsewhere in the Qur'an; here, as Maʿārif puts it, they have been condensed.

The choice of nations is not random. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that these were the strongest and most resourceful peoples of their age — superpowers whom no subdued nation could have overcome. Yet, as it puts it, when the divine chastisement overtook nations so powerful in might, wealth and number, they were killed like flies and mosquitoes. And the sequence is aimed squarely at the audience listening in Makkah: the ayat that follow address the people of the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ time with the fact that they are not more powerful in wealth, number or might than ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lūṭ or the people of Firʿawn — then how are they sitting in such a careless manner?

That is the spirit in which to read ayah 23: **"Thamūd denied the warnings."** Note where that same word surfaces again. At the close of the episode, ayah 30 delivers the refrain "Then, how was My torment and My warnings?" — the warnings they brushed aside and the punishment that arrived are named together in a single breath.

## "One of us — and we should follow him?"

Ibn Kathīr explains that the people of Thamūd denied their Messenger Ṣāliḥ, and their objection in ayah 24 was essentially about status: **"A man, alone among us — shall we follow him? Truly, then we should be in error and distress!"** Their meaning, as Ibn Kathīr renders it, was: *We would have earned failure and loss if we all submitted to a man from among us.*

Look closely at what offends them. Not the content of the message. Not his honesty — that comes later, as an accusation thrown up afterwards. What they cannot bear is the arithmetic: one man, from our own stock, and an entire nation falling in behind him.

Ayah 25 makes it explicit — **"Is it that the Reminder is sent to him alone from among us?"** Ibn Kathīr says they were amazed that the Reminder was sent to him alone among them, and it was out of that amazement that they went on to accuse him of being a liar: **"Nay, he is an insolent liar!"**

### The word *suʿur*

Their sentence in ayah 24 ends with a pair of words that Ibn Kathīr renders "in error and distress" — in the Arabic, *fī ḍalālin wa suʿur*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives this second word a short lexicological note worth pausing on. *Suʿur* appears twice in this surah. Here in ayah 24 it is Thamūd's own word, and it means "madness or insanity" — they are saying that following Ṣāliḥ would be to walk into error and lunacy. The second time, in ayah 47, the word appears in connection with the punishment of the sinners, where it is Allah's own word, and there it may also be taken in the sense of the Fire of Hell. According to lexicologists, Maʿārif notes, the word is used in both these senses.

So the mockers hurl the word at faith — and the same word returns later in the surah, in Allah's speech, describing where their rejection actually leads. The accusation and the verdict share a sound.

### "An insolent liar" — and Allah's answer

The charge in ayah 25 is heavy. Ibn Kathīr glosses **"Nay, he is an insolent liar!"** as meaning that Ṣāliḥ **"has trespassed the limits in his lies."** In their telling he is not a man who got something wrong; he is a man drunk on his own claim.

Then comes ayah 26, and Ibn Kathīr presents it as Allah the Exalted's response — and it is devastating in its economy. Allah does not argue the charge point by point. The same two descriptions simply stand again, now in Allah's speech, with the question of who they actually belong to left to time: **"Tomorrow they will come to know who is the liar, the insolent one!"** Ibn Kathīr comments that this was at once a warning, a threat, and a sure promise delivered to them.

"Tomorrow" is the mercy inside the threat. It means the file is not yet closed. There is still an interval — and what fills that interval is the she-camel.

## The she-camel: a mercy shaped like a test

Ayah 27: **"Verily, We are sending the she-camel as a test for them. So watch them, and be patient!"** The word rendered "test" here is *fitnah*.

Ibn Kathīr explains that to test and try the people of Thamūd, Allah sent them a superb, pregnant female camel that emerged from solid rock — and, crucially, *according to their request*. They had asked; Allah gave. It was to become a proof against them from Allah the Exalted, after which they were supposed to believe in what was brought to them by Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him.

That single detail reframes the whole episode. The camel is not an arbitrary trial dropped on them out of nowhere; it is the answer to their own demand. The sign was placed among them precisely so that what they did next would settle the matter.

**"So watch them, and be patient!"** Two commands to the prophet, not to the people. Ibn Kathīr unpacks them as Allah's command: *await, O Ṣāliḥ, and see what will become of them, and be patient; verily the better end will be yours and you will have success in this life and the Hereafter.* Notice what a prophet is told to do while his people are being tested: watch, and hold. Do not force the outcome. There is a whole discipline of daʿwah in those two words, and a comfort for anyone who has had to wait while people they love make their own choice.

## Water, turns, and the boredom of obedience

Ayah 28: **"And inform them that the water is to be shared between (her and) them, each one's right to drink being established (by turns)."**

Ibn Kathīr explains the arrangement plainly: one day for her to drink, and one day for them to drink. He points to the parallel wording in Sūrah ash-Shuʿarāʾ, where Ṣāliḥ says, "Here is a she-camel: it has a right to drink, and you have a right to drink (water) on a day, known" (26:155).

And it was not deprivation. Mujāhid said: **"When she did not drink, they would drink the water, and when she drank, they would drink her milk."** Nothing was taken from them. On her day they had milk instead of water. The test was not scarcity; the test was *taking turns* — accepting that something outside themselves had a claim on a resource they had always treated as simply theirs.

That is a quietly modern point. The command was not heroic. It was a rota. Faith here looked like waiting your turn at the well, day after unremarkable day, because Allah had said so. It is precisely this kind of ordinary, unglamorous obedience that pride finds hardest to swallow.

## A national crime in one short sentence

Ayah 29 is one of the shortest sentences in the passage and one of the most carefully weighted: **"But they called their comrade and he took (a sword) and killed (her)."**

Three movements, one after another, at the speed of the act itself: they called — he took — he killed.

Ibn Kathīr identifies the man: according to the Scholars of Tafsīr his name was **Qudār bin Sālif**, and he was the evilest among them. Ibn Kathīr connects him to the ayah in Sūrah ash-Shams, "When the most wicked man among them went forth (to kill the she-camel)" (91:12). On the words rendered "and he took," Ibn Kathīr's gloss is simply: meaning, to harm. The phrase by itself is almost neutral — he reached, he took it upon himself — and the horror is entirely in what came next.

But look at who the Qur'an holds responsible. The sentence does not begin with the killer. It begins with the crowd: *they called*. Only then does the hand move. And the man is named as **their comrade** — their own man, their instrument. Thamūd could have told themselves that only Qudār did it. The ayah does not allow that. Those who summon, shelter and cheer a crime are named alongside the one who commits it.

Then, immediately, ayah 30: **"Then, how was My torment and My warnings?"** Ibn Kathīr renders the sense as Allah saying: *I tormented them, so how was the torment I sent on them because of their disbelief in Me and denying My Messenger?* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this same sentence is repeated as a refrain after the punishment of each nation described in this surah. It is a question that expects no answer, only a shudder.

## One sound

Ayah 31: **"Verily, We sent against them a single Ṣayḥah, and they became like straw, Al-Muḥtaẓir."** *Ṣayḥah* is the blast or cry that came upon them.

Weigh the word "single". A people whom Maʿārif has just described as beyond the reach of any nation around them were finished by one blast. Ibn Kathīr's comment is stark: **they all perished and none of them remained.** They were no more; they died out, just as plants and grass dry and die out.

The closing image is the most vivid thing in the passage, and the bundle gives two readings of it:

- **As-Suddī** said that they became like the dry grass in the desert when it becomes burned and the wind scatters it all about.
- **Ibn Zayd** explained where the word *Al-Muḥtaẓir* comes from: "The Arabs used to erect fences (*Ḥiẓār*, from which the word *Al-Muḥtaẓir* is derived) made of dried bushes, around their camels and cattle."

Hold that against what Thamūd were. Ibn Kathīr has just described a camel that came out of solid rock; Maʿārif has just called these nations superpowers. And the ayah leaves them as dry stuff from a livestock pen. The people who quarrelled over whose turn it was at the water end as the brittle scraps of a cattle fence.

## "Then is there any that will remember?"

Ayah 32 closes the episode with the refrain that runs through the whole surah: **"And indeed, We have made the Qur'an easy to understand and remember; then is there any that will remember?"** Maʿārif renders the same ayah as, "and indeed We have made the Qur'an easy for seeking advice. So, is there one to seek advice?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why this sentence sits exactly here, after each catastrophe. It is repeated to advise the Muslims and the disbelievers in general, and it indicates that the only way to avoid the terrible chastisement is to take to the advice of the Qur'an. Allah has made the Qur'an easy *to the extent of paying heed to the admonition and warnings* — that is the specific ease being claimed. And Maʿārif's conclusion is sobering: only the most ill-fated person will not take advantage of the warnings.

Read the closing question slowly. It is not a shrug. It is put as a search — is there one, anyone, who will take the advice? Ten ayat have just shown a nation with a sign standing in front of it, drinking from its own well, that still would not.

## What this passage asks of us

Read as a whole, ayat 23–32 name three ways a heart refuses guidance, and one way out.

**Pride about the messenger, not the message (ayat 24–25).** Thamūd never engaged with what Ṣāliḥ said. They fixed on who he was — one of us, no more impressive than us — and treated that as a refutation. It is still the commonest way to escape a truth we do not want: audit the speaker until the point goes away.

**Resentment of a shared claim (ayah 28).** Their test was a schedule for a well, and their sabotage was aimed at the schedule. When faith asks something small and repeated of us — a prayer time, a portion of income, a restraint on the tongue — that is usually where the real fight is, not in the grand questions.

**Outsourcing the deed (ayah 29).** They called; he struck; the ayah names them all. Approval, encouragement and silence are not neutral positions.

**And the way out (ayat 26, 27, 32).** The warning came with "tomorrow" attached — time was given. The prophet was told to watch and be patient, and promised the better end in this life and the Hereafter. And the surah insists that the reminder has been made easy — easy, as Maʿārif says, to the extent of heeding its admonition and its warnings. The question ending ayah 32 is not rhetorical the way ayah 30 is. It is an actual question, addressed to whoever is reading, and it is still open.

passages.title: Lot's people and the storm of stones
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat tell the ruin of the people of Lūṭ (peace be upon him) — a city warned, a night of siege at a prophet's door, and a morning that came down as stones. What holds them together is a single thread running from the first word to the last: **warning**. They *denied* the warnings (33), they *disputed* the warnings (36), they were made to *taste* the warnings (37, 39) — and then the passage turns away from them and asks whether anyone else will take the warning while there is still time (40).

## Where this sits in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the design of Sūrat al-Qamar: it opens on the note that the Day of Judgement is fast approaching, so that people who are absorbed in this world and unaware of the Hereafter might come to their senses. The punishment of the Hereafter is mentioned first; then the sūrah turns to the consequences that overtook world-famous nations who opposed their prophets in this present life. Their stories are recounted in detail elsewhere in the Qur'an; here, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, they have been condensed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an observation worth pausing on: **the people of Lūṭ were the first people who were destroyed by divine punishment.** And it stresses that all of these nations were the strongest and most resourceful — it was not possible for any of the subdued nations to overcome any of these superpowers. Yet when the divine chastisement overtook them, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, these nations, so powerful in might, wealth and number, "were killed like flies and mosquitoes." That is exactly the point the sūrah is building toward: the verses that follow this passage, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, address the people of the time of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ — they are not more powerful in wealth, number and might than the people of Lūṭ, than ʿĀd and Thamūd, than the people of Firʿawn. Then how are they sitting in a careless manner?

## The crime, and why the punishment matched it

Ibn Kathīr states the case directly: the people of Lūṭ defied and denied their Messenger and committed sodomy — the awful immoral sin, he says, that no people in the history of mankind had committed before. And this, he explains, is precisely why Allah destroyed them with a type of torment that He never inflicted upon any nation before them. A crime without precedent met a punishment without precedent. The proportion is deliberate.

Ayah 33 puts it in the sūrah's shared formula: *kadhdhabat qawmu Lūṭin bi'l-nudhur* — "the people of Lot rejected the warnings." Notice what is denied. Not Lūṭ's existence, not his character — his **warnings**. The quarrel was never really about information; it was about a message that demanded they stop.

## The night at the door (ayah 37)

Ayat 36 and 37 reach back before the destruction and show us how it came. Ayah 36: *wa laqad andharahum baṭshatanā fa-tamāraw bi'l-nudhur* — rendered in the translation as, "He had already warned them of Our ˹crushing˺ blow but they disputed." Ibn Kathīr explains: before the torment struck his people, Lūṭ warned them of Allah's torment and punishment — and they did not heed the warning, nor listen to Lūṭ, but instead **doubted and disputed** it. That is the shape of their refusal. Not blank ignorance of the message, but argument against it.

Then ayah 37 gives us the night everything turned on.

**Ibn Kathīr's account.** This is the night, he says, that the angels **Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl and Isrāfīl** came to Lūṭ in the shape of handsome young men, as a test from Allah for Lūṭ's people. Lūṭ hosted his guests, while his wife — Ibn Kathīr calls her "the evil old one" — sent a message to her people informing them of Lūṭ's guests. They came to him in haste from every direction, and Lūṭ had to close the door in their faces. They came during the night and tried to break the door; Lūṭ tried to fend them off, shielding his guests from them, saying, *"These are my daughters, if you must act (so)"* (15:71) — in reference, Ibn Kathīr explains, to the women of their own community. They answered: *"Surely, you know that we have neither any desire nor need of your daughters"* (11:79) — meaning, Ibn Kathīr says, 'we do not have any desire for women' — *"and indeed you know well what we want!"* (11:79).

When the situation became serious and they insisted on coming in, Ibn Kathīr continues, **Jibrīl went out to them and struck their eyes with the tip of his wing**, causing them to lose their sight. They went back feeling for the walls to guide them, threatening Lūṭ with what would befall him in the morning.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account** tells the same night without naming the angels: the licentious people came to Lūṭ from every direction, and he had to shut the door to protect his guests; they came during the night and tried to break the door down **and to scale the walls** to come in.

That whole night is what the Qur'an compresses into *fa-ṭamasnā aʿyunahum* — "so We blinded their eyes." And notice how the act is assigned: an angel's wing moved, but Allah says *We* blinded them. The means are created; the doing is His.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records one more detail, and it is the tender part of a hard story: the immoral behaviour of his people **distressed** Lūṭ — but when the guests revealed to him that they were angels sent by Allah to inflict destructive punishment on his people, and assured him that these men would not be able to hurt them in any way, **he felt comforted**. A prophet, exhausted at a door he cannot hold much longer, is told: the door was never his to hold.

## The word *rāwadū*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the verb in ayah 37, *rāwadūhu ʿan ḍayfihi*, which it renders "they had even tried to tempt him against his guests." The word *murāwadah*, it explains, signifies to entice someone to satisfy one's lust. Ibn Kathīr renders the same phrase as their seeking to shame his guests. So the Qur'an does not merely say they attacked; it says they came at Lūṭ working on him *about his guests*. They wanted him to hand over the men under his own roof and his own protection. A violation of hospitality was stacked on top of the sin itself — and the men they were pressing him for were, as both sources make plain, angels.

## The morning (ayah 38)

*Wa laqad ṣabbaḥahum bukratan ʿadhābun mustaqirr* — "and indeed, by the early morning they were overwhelmed by an abiding torment."

They had gone home blind, threatening Lūṭ with **the morning**; the morning is exactly what arrived, and it was not theirs.

Ibn Kathīr explains the phrase "an abiding torment seized them early in the morning" to mean **a torment that they had no way of escaping or avoiding**. Not a blow that could be ridden out. Something that came down and stayed until it had finished its work.

What that torment was, Ibn Kathīr describes at ayah 34: Allah the Exalted commanded Jibrīl (peace be upon him) to raise their cities to the sky and then turn them upside down over them, followed by stones made of marked *Sijjīl*. Hence *ḥāṣib* in ayah 34 — which Ibn Kathīr renders as a violent storm of stones.

## The exception, and the reason for it (ayat 34–35)

*"…except the family of Lot, whom We saved in the last hour of the night, as a blessing from Us. This is how We reward whoever gives thanks."*

Three things here repay attention.

**First, *bi-saḥar* — the last hour of the night.** Ibn Kathīr says they left the city in the last part of the night and were saved from the torment that struck their people. Rescue and ruin were only hours apart. The saved were walking out in the last dark of the night, while the men who had besieged the door were still feeling their way home along the walls.

**Second, who was and was not included.** Ibn Kathīr notes that not one of Lūṭ's people believed in him — none of them. And Lūṭ's own wife suffered the same end as her people, while Allah's Prophet Lūṭ left Sodom with his daughters in safety, unharmed. So "the family of Lūṭ" is not a bloodline exemption. A woman inside a prophet's own house was destroyed with the city — and, as Ibn Kathīr reports, it was she who sent word to her people that Lūṭ had guests. Proximity to guidance saves nobody; response to it does.

**Third, *najzī man shakara* — "This is how We reward whoever gives thanks" (35).** This is the passage's one flash of mercy, and it is worth noticing what word Allah chose to name the saved by. Not "whoever was clever," not "whoever got out in time" — *whoever gives thanks*. Their rescue is called *niʿmah min ʿindinā*, "a blessing from Us," and thankfulness is the human posture that fits a blessing. In eight ayat about denial, the survivors are defined by gratitude.

## Why "taste" is said twice (37, 39)

Elsewhere in this sūrah, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the refrain after each ruined nation is *fa-kayfa kāna ʿadhābī wa nudhur* — "How then was My torment and My warnings?" Here, for the people of Lūṭ, the closing line is different, and it falls **twice**: *fa-dhūqū ʿadhābī wa nudhur*, "Then taste My torment and My warnings" — once after the blinding in ayah 37, and again after the morning in ayah 39.

Read in sequence, that is two sentences of judgement for two stages of judgement. The first came the night before: they were blinded, and they walked home — with hours still in hand. The second came at dawn, and of that one Ibn Kathīr says there was no way of escaping or avoiding it.

And note the pairing inside the phrase: *ʿadhābī wa nudhur* — "My torment **and My warnings**." The warnings are handed back to them alongside the punishment, because the warnings were the mercy they threw away. A man punished after being warned is tasting his own refusal.

## Ayah 40 — the sentence aimed at the reader

*"And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy to remember. So is there anyone who will be mindful?"*

Every one of these histories in the sūrah ends here, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the verse is repeated as advice to the Muslims and the disbelievers in general: **the only way to avoid that terrible chastisement is to take to the advice of the Qur'an.** Allah has made the Qur'an easy to the extent of paying heed to its admonition and its warnings. It is not locked away from you, and it is not too hard for you. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the conclusion starkly — only the most ill-fated person will not take advantage of the warnings.

So *fa-hal min muddakir* — "is there anyone who will take heed?" — is not a request for information. It is an invitation left standing open, again and again, after every ruined city.

## Living it

**Warnings are a mercy, and what we do with them is the whole test.** This nation did not lack information; they had a prophet among them warning them of Allah's torment and punishment (36). What they did with it, in Ibn Kathīr's words, was doubt and dispute it. A warning we argue with rather than act on has already done us no good.

**Gratitude is a rescuing posture (35).** The people led out of that city are named for their thankfulness. *Shukr* here — thankfulness — is not a phrase said after food; it is the whole stance of someone who knows that any good he has is *min ʿindinā*, from Allah, and who lives accordingly.

**Being near the truth is not the same as being with it.** Lūṭ's wife lived in the house of a prophet and met the same end as her people. That is a sober check on anyone who assumes a family, a community or a lineage will carry them.

**The door you cannot hold was never yours to hold.** Lūṭ was distressed at his own threshold, with the crowd pressing in from every direction, and his relief came not from winning the standoff but from learning who his guests were and Who had sent them. The believer does what he can at the door and leaves the outcome with Allah.

**And the Qur'an has been made easy — so use it (40).** These eight ayat exist so that a city need not be destroyed twice for the lesson to land. The passage is finally addressed not to Sodom, but to whoever is reading it.

passages.title: Pharaoh's people, and the challenge to Quraysh
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat close the sūrah's long procession of destroyed nations with the mightiest of them all — Pharaoh's people — and then turn the whole argument around to face the Quraysh sitting in Makkah listening to it. The unity of the passage is that pivot: ayat 41–42 are history, ayat 43–46 are the cross-examination of a living audience, and the hinge is a single question — *what makes you think you are the exception?*

## Where this comes in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the shape of the whole sūrah, and it explains why this passage lands the way it does. Sūrah al-Qamar opens on the note that the Day of Judgement is fast approaching, addressed to people whose appetite for this world has left them unaware of the Hereafter. Punishment in the Hereafter is mentioned first; then the Qur'an turns to the consequences that overtook earlier nations in *this* life — among them the people of Lūṭ (peace be upon him), whom Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes were the first people destroyed by divine punishment, the tribes of ʿĀd and Thamūd, and now the people of Pharaoh. Their histories are recounted in detail elsewhere in the Qur'an; here they are condensed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a point about these five nations that is easy to miss: every one of them was among the strongest and most resourceful of peoples. It was not possible for any of the subdued nations to overcome any of these superpowers — and every one of them was destroyed by divine punishment. That is exactly why, after each account, the sūrah repeats **فَكَيْفَ كَانَ عَذَابِي وَنُذُرِ** — *"How then was My torment and My warnings?"* Nations very powerful in might, wealth and number were killed, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, like flies and mosquitoes. And alongside that refrain runs the other one, **وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ فَهَلْ مِن مُّدَّكِرٍ** — *"and indeed We have made the Qur'an easy for seeking advice. So, is there one to seek advice?"* — because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, the only way to avoid that terrible chastisement is to take to the advice of the Qur'an. Allah has made it easy to the extent of paying heed to the admonition and warnings; only the most ill-fated person will not take advantage of them.

So when ayah 41 begins, the reader has already been shown the ruins of nation after nation. Pharaoh's people are the last of the five.

## Ayat 41–42: the warnings came to Pharaoh's people

**"And indeed, the warnings came to the people of Pharaoh."** Ibn Kathir tells the story compactly. A Messenger came to them from Allah — Mūsā, supported by his brother Hārūn. Their message carried both halves of what a prophet brings: good news if the people believed, and a warning if they rejected the message. Allah supported Mūsā and Hārūn with tremendous miracles and great signs.

Notice the word for what came to them: **النُّذُر** (*al-nudhur*), the warnings — the same word that runs through the sūrah's refrain, *"How then was My torment and My warnings?"* Pharaoh's court was not left guessing. Tremendous miracles and great signs had been placed in front of them.

Ayah 42 records the response in the bluntest possible terms: **كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا كُلِّهَا** — *"(They) denied all Our signs."* Ibn Kathir underlines that *all*: Mūsā and Hārūn were supported with great signs, "but Fir'awn and his people rejected all of them." It was not that one miracle was disputed and another accepted. Every sign, without exception, was called a lie. That total rejection is what makes what follows proportionate.

**فَأَخَذْنَاهُمْ أَخْذَ عَزِيزٍ مُّقْتَدِرٍ** — *"so We seized them with a punishment of the Almighty, All-Capable."* The Arabic is a construction that measures the act by the One who performs it: a seizing of the kind that belongs to the All-Mighty, the All-Capable. Ibn Kathir puts it exactly that way — "Allah took them the way the All-Mighty, the All-Capable would."

What such a seizure looks like, Ibn Kathir states without softening: "He destroyed them all leaving none surviving to tell the story of what happened to them." Not one of them was left to give an account of it.

## Ayat 43–44: the questions turned on Quraysh

Now the address swings around. Ibn Kathir reads ayah 43 as spoken directly to the pagans of Makkah: **أَكُفَّارُكُمْ** — *"Are your disbelievers…"* — meaning, in his words, 'O idolators of the Quraysh'; **خَيْرٌ مِّنْ أُولَٰئِكُمْ** — "better than these?", meaning better than the nations mentioned here, "who were destroyed on account of their disbelief in the Messengers and rejecting the Scriptures." Are *you* better than these?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the same question as the natural continuation of those accounts: the people of the time of the Prophet ﷺ are not more powerful in terms of wealth, number and might than the people of Lūṭ (peace be upon him), the tribes of ʿĀd and Thamūd, or the people of Pharaoh. Then how are they sitting in such a careless manner? The argument is not an insult; it is arithmetic. If the strong were not spared, on what basis does the weaker party feel safe?

**أَمْ لَكُم بَرَاءَةٌ فِي الزُّبُرِ** — *"Or have you immunity in the Divine Scriptures?"* Ibn Kathir paraphrases the question: 'do you have immunity from Allah that the torment and punishment will not touch you?' The question is deliberately impossible to answer: has some revealed book issued you an exemption from the law that levelled every nation before you?

On **الزُّبُر** (*al-zubur*), Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the lexical note: *zubur* is the plural of *zabūr*, which stands for any written book, and which specifically refers to the Scripture that was revealed to the Prophet Dāwūd (peace be upon him). So the challenge is to produce it from the record — from anything ever written down by revelation. There is nothing to produce.

Ayah 44 then quotes their actual state of mind: **أَمْ يَقُولُونَ نَحْنُ جَمِيعٌ مُّنتَصِرٌ** — *"Or say they: 'We are a great multitude, victorious?'"* Ibn Kathir explains what they meant: they believed they would support each other, and that their great gathering would avail them against those who intend to harm them. This is the real answer to the previous question. They had no written immunity; what they had was *numbers* — mutual support, a united front, the confidence of a crowd. That was their theology of safety.

It is worth pausing on the irony. The passage has just recited nations that, on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own description, no subdued people could have overcome — and Quraysh's defence is strength in numbers.

## Ayah 45: the promise, and the day it was kept

**سَيُهْزَمُ الْجَمْعُ وَيُوَلُّونَ الدُّبُرَ** — *"Their multitude will be put to flight, and they will show their backs."* (The ayah is also rendered: *"˹Soon˺ their united front will be defeated and ˹forced to˺ flee."*) Ibn Kathir: Allah responded to their boast by affirming that "their gathering shall scatter, and they shall be defeated."
