The very thing they had named as their security — the gathering — is the thing the ayah says will be put to flight.

Ibn Kathir then attaches this ayah to one of the most vivid scenes in the Prophet's ﷺ life. Al-Bukhari recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said: the Prophet ﷺ, while in a dome-shaped tent on the day of the battle of Badr, said,

> **أَنْشُدُكَ عَهْدَكَ وَوَعْدَكَ، اللّٰهُمَّ إِنْ شِئْتَ لَمْ تُعْبَدْ بَعْدَ الْيَوْمِ فِي الْأَرْضِ أَبَدًا**
>
> "O Allah! I ask you for the fulfillment of Your covenant and promise. O Allah! If You wish (to destroy the believers), You will never be worshipped on the earth after today."

Abū Bakr caught him by the hand and said, "This is sufficient, O Allah's Messenger! You have sufficiently asked and petitioned Allah." The Prophet ﷺ was clad in his armour at that time and went out, saying:

> **سَيُهْزَمُ الْجَمْعُ وَيُوَلُّونَ الدُّبُرَ ۖ بَلِ السَّاعَةُ مَوْعِدُهُمْ وَالسَّاعَةُ أَدْهَىٰ وَأَمَرُّ**
>
> "Their multitude will be put to flight and they will show their backs. Nay, but the Hour is their appointed time and that Hour will be more grievous and more bitter."

Read that sequence slowly. The Prophet ﷺ is asking Allah for one thing — the fulfillment of Allah's own covenant and promise. He is not inventing a hope; he is holding to the word Allah had already given. And what he recites as he steps out in his armour is not a battle-cry of his own composition but the ayah itself, spoken as though the outcome were already recorded. That is what it looks like to take a Qur'anic promise as a fact you can lean your whole weight on.

## Ayah 46: but the real appointment is later

**بَلِ السَّاعَةُ مَوْعِدُهُمْ وَالسَّاعَةُ أَدْهَىٰ وَأَمَرُّ** — *"Nay, but the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour will be more grievous and more bitter."*

The ayah lifts the reader's eyes past the battlefield. Defeat in the field is real, but the Hour is what they are actually appointed to.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the two closing words. **أَدْهَىٰ** (*adhā*) means "more" or "most calamitous." **أَمَرُّ** (*amarr*) is derived from *murr*, which originally means "bitter"; by extension anything difficult or painful is also referred to as *amarr* and *murr*. So the Hour is greater as a catastrophe and harder as an experience — bitter, not merely large in scale. A rout in the field is over by sunset; the Hour is not.

And there is a striking historical note on this exact ayah. Al-Bukhari also recorded that Yūsuf bin Māhak said: "I was with the Mother of the faithful, ʿĀʾishah, when she said, 'When I was still a young playful girl in Makkah, this ayah was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ: *Nay, but the Hour is their appointed time and that Hour will be more grievous and more bitter*.'" Ibn Kathir notes that this is the abridged narration collected by Al-Bukhari, who also collected a longer narration of it in the Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an, and that Muslim did not collect this hadith.

Put the two reports side by side and the passage acquires a second dimension. ʿĀʾishah places the revelation in Makkah, when she was still a young girl. The Ibn ʿAbbās report places the recitation on the day of Badr — where, as Ibn Kathir says, the gathering did scatter and they were defeated, exactly as the ayah had affirmed. The words did not change; events caught up with them.

## Living it

**Numbers are not a defence.** Quraysh's confidence — that they would support each other and that their great gathering would avail them — is one of the most ordinary human securities there is: the reassurance of belonging to the winning side. Ayah 45 dismantles it in a few words. Whatever crowd a person is trusting in, the crowd is not what decides.

**No one holds an exemption.** Ayah 43's question — do you have immunity in the Scriptures? — is worth turning inward as well as outward. Nobody has been granted immunity from Allah such that the torment and punishment will not touch them. The nations of this sūrah were not weaker than us; if strength did not shield them, nothing shields anyone but Allah's mercy.

**Hold to Allah's promise the way the Prophet ﷺ did.** In the tent at Badr he asked for the fulfillment of a covenant and a promise already given, and then walked out reciting the very ayah that contained it. Believing a Qur'anic promise means being willing to act on it before you can see it.

**Keep the Hour in view.** Ayah 46 refuses to let even a great victory become the horizon. Any worldly reckoning, however severe, is smaller and shorter than the appointment that is *adhā wa amarr*. And as the sūrah keeps insisting between each ruined nation, the way to avoid that chastisement is to take to the advice of a Qur'an that Allah Himself has made easy — *so, is there one to seek advice?*

passages.title: The wicked dragged into Fire; all is decreed
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move from a picture of the guilty being hauled into the Fire (47–48) straight into one of the great creedal statements of the Qur'an: that Allah created everything by a measure (49), and that when He commands, the thing is done in less time than a blink (50). What holds them together is an occasion recorded in the tafsir literature: the idolaters of the Quraysh came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arguing with him and discounting the decree, and these ayat came down. The threat and the doctrine of *qadar* are set side by side — and then the passage adds that the Power which measures out all things executes its word instantly.

## Ayah 47: lost — and burning, or mad

Allah says the *mujrimūn* — rendered "the wicked" or "the criminals" — are **fī ḍalālin wa suʿur**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *ḍalāl* carries its familiar sense of "error" or "deviation": they have wandered off the road.

The second word, *suʿur*, is read two ways, and the difference is worth feeling:

- **The Fire.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *suʿur* in this context means "the Hell-Fire" — and Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah reads: "the criminals are in error and will burn."
- **Madness.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records this as the other meaning of the word, and it is the reading the translation above follows: their rejection is not clear-headed dissent but a kind of derangement.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents the first as "according to one interpretation" and the second as the other meaning of the word; neither cancels the other. Ibn Kathir's reading of the whole phrase draws them together: the criminals are "misguided away from the truth and engulfed in confusion, because of the doubts and uncertainty they are in." That is the inner state the ayah is diagnosing — not settled disbelief so much as a mind churning in doubt, suspicion and hesitation, unable to come to rest anywhere.

Ibn Kathir then makes a sobering extension: **this description "befits every disbeliever and innovator of all types and forms of sects."** The ayah is not a museum piece about seventh-century Mecca. Wherever a person's relationship to revealed truth becomes permanent doubt and self-invented religion, the description applies.

## Ayah 48: the punishment shaped like the crime

**يَوْمَ يُسْحَبُونَ فِي النَّارِ عَلَىٰ وُجُوهِهِمْ** — "the Day they will be dragged into the Fire on their faces."

Ibn Kathir's comment on this ayah is one of those observations that, once seen, cannot be unseen. The punishment is the exact outward shape of the inward sin:

> "Just as they were consumed in doubt, suspicion and hesitation, they ended up in the Fire. And just as they were misguided, they will end up being dragged on their faces, unaware of where they will be taken."

Look at the correspondence Ibn Kathir draws. In this world they were *lost* — and on that Day they are dragged face-down, "unaware of where they will be taken." Their blindness becomes their transport. They chose not to look; now they are given a journey in which looking is impossible.

And they are *dragged*. Not summoned, not marched — hauled, the way a thing is moved rather than a person. The face, which a human being instinctively protects and by which he is known and honoured, is the part put to the ground.

Then comes the rebuke: **ذُوقُوا مَسَّ سَقَرَ** — "Taste the touch of Saqar," which Ibn Kathir's text renders "Taste you the touch of Hell!" He says that at this moment they "will be admonished and criticized" — the physical torment arrives wrapped in reproach. Note the restraint of the wording: not "taste the Fire," but taste its **touch** — the merest contact. If the brush of it is this, what is the whole?

## Ayah 49: the argument at the Prophet's ﷺ door

Here the passage turns, and to understand why, you need the occasion of revelation — which both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān place at the centre of this ayah.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Hurayrah: *"The idolators of the Quraysh came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arguing with him and discounting the Qadar,"* and this ayah was revealed. Ibn Kathir notes that **Muslim, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah** collected this hadith; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites it from the *Musnad* of Ahmad, Sahih Muslim and Tirmidhi, describing them as "debating and arguing with him on the question of *taqdir*."

So picture it. A delegation arrives not to ask but to argue — disputing the decree. The answer that comes down is not a philosophical treatise. It is placed immediately after the image of men dragged on their faces: **إِنَّا كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقْنَاهُ بِقَدَرٍ** — "Indeed, We have created everything by a measure."

Two further reports narrow the target. Al-Bazzar recorded from 'Amr bin Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that these ayat "were revealed about those who deny Al-Qadar." And Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Zurarah, from his father, that the Prophet ﷺ recited *"Taste you the touch of Hell! Verily, We have created all things with Qadar"* and then said that these ayat were revealed about some members of his Ummah who would come before the end of time and deny Allah's decree. Ibn Kathir also records, from Nafi', that 'Abdullah bin 'Umar heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, **"There will be some members of my Ummah who will deny Al-Qadar"** — a hadith Imam Ahmad recorded and Abu Dawud collected from him.

In other words: the ayah was revealed for a specific dispute, and the Prophet ﷺ himself indicated it was aimed past that dispute at a controversy still in the future.

## What *qadar* actually means

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word carefully, and gives it two layers.

**The literal layer: measure and proportion.** *Qadar* first means "measure" — to create something with a proper measure and proportion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it is possible for this literal sense to apply here: Allah is the Supreme Sage who created every species of existing thing wisely and with proper measurement, big and small, in different shapes and sizes, and who then *maintains* the structure of each individual by that same wise measurement. It points to your own hand as the exhibit: the fingers and toes are not equal in size, the lengths differ, the length and breadth of hands and legs are wisely structured, and their bones, muscles and skins are created flexible enough to stretch and contract. "When we analyze every single part of every single limb and organ of [human] body, we discern the wondrous vistas of Divine wisdom opening up."

Something quietly powerful happens when you notice that this is the *same word* as the theological one. Measurement, not caprice, is the root sense the word carries.

**The theological layer: taqdīr.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that as a theological term *qadar* is used in the sense of *taqdīr* — divine predetermination — and that most authorities on tafsir, on account of the hadith reports above, take it in that sense here. On that reading: Allah has predetermined the total sum of everything; He created everything with predestined limits before the things themselves were created; He knew everything that would occur before it occurred, and recorded everything — time and place, growth and decline — before it occurred. Everything that occurs in this world occurs according to the Divine Plan worked out in eternity-without-beginning.

Ibn Kathir links the ayah to two others that carry the same word: *"He has created everything, and has measured it exactly according to its due measurements"* (25:2), and *"Who has created, and then proportioned it. And Who has measured and then guided"* (87:1–3) — which he glosses as: He measured out the total sum of everything, and then guided the creation to it. Measure first; guidance to the measure after.

## What the Imams of the Sunnah built on this ayah

Ibn Kathir states plainly that "the Imams of the Sunnah relied on this honorable Ayah as evidence that Allah created the creation with destined limits before they were created," adding that "He knew everything that will occur before it occurred and recorded everything that will occur, before they occurred." They used this ayah, and similar ayat and hadiths, to refute the **Qadariyyah** — a sect, he says, that "started their sect during the latter time of the Companions." (He mentions treating the subject in detail in his explanation of the chapter on faith of Sahih Al-Bukhari.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jamāʿah with a distinction worth keeping straight, because people flatten it: *taqdīr* is one of the affirmed and standard articles of faith in Islam; anyone who denies it outright "is an atheist or goes out of the pale of Islam," while the sects that deny it by convoluted or twisted interpretation are counted as *fāsiq* — sinners or transgressors. Two different verdicts for two different things.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir gathers a cluster of hadiths on this ayah. Taken together they show that *qadar* was never taught as an abstraction — it was taught as something that changes how you speak, how you grieve, and how you act.

- **'Abdullah bin 'Umar** reported the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying, *"Every thing is predetermined, even laziness and intelligence."* Imam Ahmad recorded it, and Muslim collected it using a chain of narration through Imam Malik. Even the qualities we most take credit or blame for sit inside the measure.

- There is an authentic hadith, Ibn Kathir says, in which the Messenger of Allah taught: *"Seek the help of Allah and do not succumb to feebleness. And when an affliction strikes you, say: 'Allah has decreed this, and He does as He wills.' Do not say: 'Had I done this or that, this or that would have happened' — because 'if' opens the door wide for the work of Ash-Shaytan."* Notice that the belief is presented as an antidote to a specific torment: the endless replaying of what you might have done differently.

- In a hadith from 'Abbas, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: *"Know that if the Ummah were to all gather their strength to cause you some benefit that Allah has not decreed for you, they will never be able to bring you that benefit. And if they gather their strength to bring a harm to you that Allah has not written on you, they will never be able to harm you. The pens have gone dry and the Books of Record have been closed."*

- **'Ubadah**, ill and thought by his son to be dying, asked to be helped upright and said: *"O my son! Know that you will not taste the delight of Faith or earn true knowledge in Allah until you believe in Al-Qadar, the good and the not so good parts of it."* Asked how one *knows* this, he answered with a definition anyone can carry: *"When you know that what has missed you, would never have come to you and what has befallen you would never have missed you."* Then he narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: *"The first thing Allah created was the Pen, right after that commanded it, 'Record!' and the Pen recorded everything that will occur until the Day of Resurrection."* He closed with a warning to his son: if you die not having this belief, you will enter the Hellfire. Imam Ahmad recorded this; At-Tirmidhi also recorded it and said: "Hasan Sahih Gharib."

- It is confirmed in **Sahih Muslim**, from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Verily, Allah recorded the measurements for the creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and earth."* Ibn Wahb added: *"And His Throne was over the water."* At-Tirmidhi also recorded it and said: "Hasan, Sahih Gharib."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a tradition recorded by Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Tabarani, on the authority of 'Abdullah Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Some members of every community are Magians, and the Magians of my Ummah are those who deny taqdīr. If they fall ill, do not visit them; and if they die, do not attend their funerals."* (cited via *Rūh al-Maʿānī*.)

**How seriously the Companions took it.** 'Ata' bin Abi Rabah reported that he went to Ibn 'Abbas and found him drawing water from the well of Zamzam, the bottom of his clothes wet, and told him that people had begun to talk against the decree — some denying it. Ibn 'Abbas asked, "Have they done this?" — and when told yes, swore by Allah that this very ayah was revealed only about them, called them "the worst members of this Ummah," and said they were not to be visited in illness nor prayed over at death.

## Ayah 50: one command, quicker than a blink

**وَمَا أَمْرُنَا إِلَّا وَاحِدَةٌ كَلَمْحٍ بِالْبَصَرِ** — "Our command is but a single word, done in the blink of an eye."

Ibn Kathir explains this as information about the execution of Allah's will in His creation: *"We only command a thing once, without needing to repeat the command; and whatever We command comes to existence faster than the blinking of an eye without any delay, not even for an instant."*

Two things are being ruled out at once. **Repetition** — a command given twice implies the first was not sufficient, and Ibn Kathir's wording is explicit that no repetition is needed. And **delay** — "not even for an instant."

Ibn Kathir places this ayah under a heading of his own: *A Warning to beware of Allah's Threats*. That is worth pausing on. The two ayat stand together: everything is created by a measure (49) — and the command that carries it out is single and instantaneous (50). Whatever Allah has warned of does not wait on machinery being assembled. It needs one word.

The comparison chosen is also merciful in its ordinariness: *lamḥ bi'l-baṣar*, the twinkling of an eye. The fastest thing you personally know is the fastest thing you can imagine — and the ayah says Allah's command outruns it.

## Living it

The passage does not leave belief in the decree as a topic to have opinions about. From what these commentaries draw out, it lands in three places:

**In your speech.** The Prophet ﷺ taught a formula for the moment affliction hits — *"Allah has decreed this, and He does as He wills"* — and forbade its opposite, the "had I done this or that" that reopens the wound and, he ﷺ said, opens the door wide for the work of Ash-Shaytan. Grief is allowed; endless counterfactual rehearsal is not.

**In your effort.** The same hadith begins *"Seek the help of Allah and do not succumb to feebleness."* Belief in the measure is paired, in the Prophet's ﷺ own words, with the command to strive while leaning on Allah's help.

**In your fear of people.** If the whole Ummah gathering could not deliver you a benefit unwritten for you, nor a harm unwritten against you, then the leverage other people appear to hold over you is mostly imaginary. "The pens have gone dry and the Books of Record have been closed."

And beneath all three, 'Ubadah's test: *what missed you was never going to reach you; what reached you was never going to miss you.* He named this as what stands between a person and tasting the delight of faith — which tells you that this doctrine, so often argued about coldly, was meant to be experienced as relief.

passages.title: Recorded deeds and the righteous before the Sovereign
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close Sūrah al-Qamar. After a long procession of destroyed nations, the sūrah gathers everything into one final contrast: a warning drawn from history, a reminder that every deed is written down, and then, in the last two ayat, the destination of those who had taqwā — seated in truth, near the Sovereign.

What holds the passage together is the theme of **writing**. Ayat 52–53 say that everything those nations did is recorded, small and large alike; ayat 54–55 say where that record leaves the ones who took the warning to heart. The sequence moves from the ledger to the seat.

## Ayah 51 — "We have destroyed your likes"

**وَلَقَدْ أَهْلَكْنَا أَشْيَاعَكُمْ** — "And indeed, We have destroyed your likes." Ibn Kathir explains *ashyāʿakum* as **the earlier nations who denied their Messengers**.

Notice how the address works. It does not say "their likes" — it says "*your* likes." Those vanished peoples, whose stories this sūrah has just recounted one after another, are described as being of a kind with the ones now being addressed. Same objections, same confidence, same end. Ibn Kathir cites a parallel from elsewhere in the Qur'an: "And a barrier will be set between them and that which they desire, as was done in the past with the people of their kind" (34:54).

Then the sūrah repeats its refrain: **فَهَلْ مِن مُّدَّكِرٍ** — "then is there any that will remember?" Ibn Kathir glosses it precisely: *is there any that will receive admonition by remembering the humiliation and torment that Allah decreed for them?* The question is not asking for information. It is a door held open. History has already supplied the evidence; all that remains is for one person to take it to heart.

The ruins are not museum pieces. They are a mirror.

## Ayat 52–53 — The book that misses nothing

**وَكُلُّ شَيْءٍ فَعَلُوهُ فِي الزُّبُرِ** — "And everything they have done is noted in *az-Zubur*." Ibn Kathir explains *az-Zubur* as **the Books of Record entrusted to the angels, peace be upon them**. Every act of those destroyed nations is on file. What befell them in this world did not close the account.

Then ayah 53 removes the last hiding place: **وَكُلُّ صَغِيرٍ وَكَبِيرٍ مُّسْتَطَرٌ** — "And everything, small and large, is written down." Ibn Kathir takes *small and large* to mean **of their actions**, and says of *mustaṭar*: *everything that they do is recorded and written in their Record of deeds, which leaves nothing, whether large or small, but it is recorded and counted.*

Notice the order — **small first**. We instinctively assume the big deeds are what get written and the small ones evaporate. The ayah reverses that intuition before we can settle into it. And it says *everything*, which cuts both ways: the small good is no more lost than the small ill.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir brings here a narration recorded by Imam Ahmad from ʿĀ'ishah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "O ʿĀ'ishah! Beware of small sins, because there is someone assigned by Allah who records them."

An-Nasā'ī and Ibn Mājah also collected this hadith.

That single sentence is the practical heart of the passage. The danger of a small sin is not its weight but its invisibility to us — and its perfect visibility to the one who writes. Nothing is too minor to enter the ledger.

## Ayah 54 — The turn

**إِنَّ الْمُتَّقِينَ فِي جَنَّاتٍ وَنَهَرٍ** — "Verily, those who have *taqwā* will be in the midst of Gardens and Rivers." *Taqwā* is the mindfulness of Allah that makes a person careful — careful, among other things, about what goes into that record.

Ibn Kathir places this deliberately against everything that came before: **unlike the end that the miserable are facing** — loss, confusion, and being dragged in the Fire on their faces, as well as being disgraced, punished and threatened. The sūrah has spent verse after verse on destruction and on faces dragged in the Fire. Then, in a single ayah, everything opens out into gardens and flowing water.

## Ayah 55 — Seated in truth before the Sovereign

**فِي مَقْعَدِ صِدْقٍ** — "In a seat of truth," rendered in our translation as "at the Seat of Honour." Ibn Kathir explains it as being **in the Dwelling of Allah's honour, encompassed by His pleasure, His favours, His bounties, His generosity and His compassion.**

Sit with the contrast the sūrah has built. The deniers were *dragged*; these are *seated*. And the seat is one *of ṣidq*, of truth — nothing false in it, no illusion, no promise that will not hold. Everything the deniers grasped at in this world gave way beneath them.

**عِندَ مَلِيكٍ مُّقْتَدِرٍ** — "near the *Muqtadir* King," the Most Powerful Sovereign. Ibn Kathir explains this as being **with the Magnificent King who created everything and measured its destiny; He is able to grant them whatever they wish and ask for.**

Feel how that closes the circle. The very King whose measure and decree the sūrah has been describing — the one before whom nation after nation fell — is described here as *able to grant them whatever they wish and ask for*. It is one power seen from two positions: terror from one end of the sūrah, generosity from the other. And the ayah does not merely place them in a garden; it places them *near the King*. Nearness is the honour.

## From the Sunnah: who is brought near

Ibn Kathir ends his commentary on this sūrah with a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Verily, the just will be with Allah on podiums of light, to the right of ar-Raḥmān — and both of His Hands are right. They are those who are just and fair in their judgement, and with their families, and those whom they are responsible for."

Muslim and An-Nasā'ī also recorded this hadith.

Notice *who* is described as being near. The hadith attaches that nearness to those who are **just** — and after their judgement it names the small arenas: your family, and whoever is under your care. That is the same instinct as ayah 53. The record is made of small things. So, it seems, is the seat of truth.

## Living it

The passage asks a few concrete things of a believer.

**Take the warning personally.** Ayah 51 says *your* likes. When you read of nations destroyed, the intended reaction is not curiosity but the *muddakir* response — remembering, and being admonished by, what happened to people who behaved as you may be tempted to behave.

**Respect the small.** Ayah 53 and the hadith of ʿĀ'ishah together dismantle the idea of a sin too trivial to matter, because there is someone assigned by Allah who records it. The believer who takes this in stops sorting deeds into "counts" and "doesn't count."

**Be just where no one is watching.** The hadith about the podiums of light does not name rulers of empires first; it names people who are fair in their judgement, with their families, and with those in their care. That is where nearness is earned.

And keep the last ayah in view while you do. The sūrah that has thundered with destruction chooses to end not on the Fire but on gardens, rivers, a seat of truth, and nearness to a King who is able to grant His guests whatever they wish and ask for. That is where the whole sūrah has been heading.
